new_statements.quote: Stress is not contrastive in Far Western Muria. Stress is phonetically realized by loudness, a rise in pitch and a slight lengthening of the vowel of the stressed syllable. Words can carry primary stress on the first syllable. And while this is particularly true for words whose first syllable nucleus is filled by a long vowel, in some sentence frames word-final syllables can carry the primary stress. In particular, with words whose first syllable nuclei are filled by short vowels and whose second syllable onset is phonetically a tap or a flap, primary stress is not only (a) carried by the word-final syllable, but also (b) the word-initial syllable loses its syllabicity and (c) the second syllable vowel is lengthened.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive; primary stress falls on the first syllable of the word (sec. 2.4 p. 6: 'In general, words carry primary stress on the first syllable'). Exception class: disyllables with a short first vowel and a tap/flap onset to the second syllable (e.g. /uṛm/ 'louse', /taras/ 'snake') may in some sentence frames take final stress, with the first vowel reduced to non-syllabic and the second vowel lengthened, so the word is effectively monosyllabic and the long vowel is again in the first syllable. Contrastive vowel length is confined to the first syllable of non-compound words. The half-lengthening/gemination of medial consonants is conditioned by first-syllable stress (sec. 2.1.4, p. 4).
new_statements.exceptions: Final-syllable primary stress 'in some sentence frames and for some phonological word types', specifically words with short V1 + tap/flap onset of syllable 2 (p. 6, p. 67); pronunciation of such words is variable (p. 67).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (isolated elicited words from a 1100-word corpus, Kurkheda tehsil dialect, 2004-2008); the final-stress variant is said to depend on 'sentence frames'. Stress is marked in the transcription only in secs 2.3 and 9.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes Far Western Muria (Gaita Koitor Boli), ISO fmu = Glottolog farw1235, dialect of Kurkheda tehsil, Gadchiroli district, Maharashtra - a sibling Muria language-level languoid, NOT Western Muria west2408 (ISO mut) itself. For west2408 proper: Natarajan 1985 (the Glottolog-listed grammar; actually Abujhmaria/Hill Maria of Abujhmar hills, Narainpur tahsil, Bastar) is accessible and silent on stress (juncture and clause terminals are its only suprasegmentals, p. 33); If the catalog keys strictly on west2408, treat this as a sibling-variety placeholder pending Andres.

new_statements.quote: p. 27: "There are a few general rules that govern the pronunciation of these forms. i) Primary stress always fall on the first syllable of a word," | pp. 123-124: "The first stress rule places heavy stress on the first syllable of every word and on the first syllable of the second member of a compound word, hence it applies iteratively to as many segments as meet the structural conditions for its application. The second rule reduces the stress on the second element of a compound word." | p. 37 fn.: "the first element of such compounds takes stronger stress on its first syllable than the second element does. ... since it is only the first syllable of a word that gets major stress."

new_statements.relation_note: Language not in catalog (no catalog_records). The only existing statement (Mathew & Mathew 2013, primary stress on the first syllable, non-contrastive) is about Far Western Muria [fmu] = farw1235, a sibling variety; Andres describes west2408 proper (Muria Gondi of Sonspal village, Narayanpur Tahsil, Bastar) and gives the same initial-stress placement, adding an explicit rule formalism and compound secondary stress. This is the first stress statement for west2408 itself.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed and non-contrastive: primary (heavy) stress falls on the first syllable of every word (P.R.1 Stress Placement). In compounds the first syllable of the second member also receives stress, which P.R.2 reduces to secondary. Vowel length is contrastive only in initial (stressed) syllables; long vowels are reduced in unstressed syllables (P.R.6-8).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress only on the first syllable of the second element of a compound word (P.R.2 Stress Reduction; e.g. [padd-avvin] 'pig-meat' with primary on padd-, secondary on av-); no rhythmic secondary stress described for simplex words.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress placement ('always'). Related notes: certain bound forms (e.g. the feminine classifier with kinship terms) are 'weakly stressed'; the exceptions discussed in sec. 1.1.2 concern vowel length, not stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Andres 1977 describes 'the variety of Muria Gondi spoken in the Narayanpur Tahsil of Bastar District.. the particular sub-dialect.. spoken in Sonspal, a village.. about fifteen kilometres east of Narayanpur' (Introduction p. 1) = Western Muria west2408 [mut] proper (Glottolog language code Narayanpur = North Bastar Gondi = Muria-Western). The existing statement from Mathew & Mathew 2013 is about Far Western Muria [fmu] farw1235 (Gadchiroli, Maharashtra), not this variety.

sources.note: Sec. 2.4 'Non-contrastive Stress' (p. 6) and sec. 9 'Stress' (p. 67): stress is not contrastive; primary stress on the first syllable (esp. when V1 is long); in some sentence frames, and in words with a short V1 and a tap/flap onset of syllable 2, primary stress falls on the final syllable with V1 losing syllabicity and V2 lengthening. Describes Far Western Muria [fmu] = farw1235 (Kurkheda tehsil, Gadchiroli, Maharashtra), not west2408 proper.

sources.note: Silent. Phonology chapter 2 (pp. 32-84) posits 20 consonants, 10 vowels and 'Transition Features' consisting only of juncture (close / open /+/) and clause terminals (falling, rising, level) on p. 33; no occurrence of 'stress' or 'accent' anywhere in either the archive.org scanned or the Acrobat text layer. Data are Hill Maria (Abujhmaria) of Nendar village, Abujhmar hills, Narainpur tahsil, Bastar. Glottolog files this under west2408. Bibliography (pp. 317ff) names Andres 1977, Shesh 1965, Gordon 1968/1969/1976 as the only other Abujhmaria/Muria phonology sources.
